variants.name: System.Lazy<T> value holder
variants.implementation_notes: The BCL provides the holder: System.Lazy<T> wraps a Func<T> and runs it on first Value access, with LazyThreadSafetyMode deciding the policy - ExecutionAndPublication (default) synchronizes and caches the factory's exception, PublicationOnly lets threads race and never caches a failure, None skips synchronization. Lazy<T> replaces the hand-written holder and turns the failure policy into an explicit constructor argument; for mapped entities the provider's lazy-loading proxies are the same idea owned by the ORM (sibling variant).
pitfalls: ExecutionAndPublication caches the factory's exception: after one transient database failure every later access rethrows the same exception unless the factory retries internally or PublicationOnly is chosen.
Accessing Value from serialization, ToString or debugging triggers the query; Lazy<T> is not transparent to serializers, so a DTO projection remains the way to keep a payload cheap.
The deferred load still needs a live DbContext: reading Value after the scope is disposed throws ObjectDisposedException rather than a lazy-load error.

variants.name: EF Core lazy-loading proxies over virtual navigations
variants.implementation_notes: The ORM owns the marker: install Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies, call UseLazyLoadingProxies, and mark navigation properties virtual - EF Core materialises proxy subclasses that run the query through the DbContext when a navigation is read, so the mapping is the only configuration. Choose it when the model may depend on EF Core and use cases genuinely read associations unpredictably; where the needed shape is known, Include/projection is cheaper and avoids proxies altogether.
pitfalls: Only virtual navigations are intercepted: a non-virtual property is never deferred, and sealed classes cannot be proxied at all.
Every navigation read is a round trip: serializing a list of books with their authors produces N+1 unless projections or Include are used first.
